summary: Retires and obsoletes the Tao of the IETF as an IETF-maintained document, and obsoletes RFC 6722, which described its publication process. It gives the reasons for the retirement and keeps the last version of the Tao in an appendix. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Tao was the booklet that explained to newcomers how the IETF works, what a working group does and how a document becomes a standard. It was first published in 1993 and was revised only a handful of times, so it drifted out of date. This RFC retires it, and says that the same material is now on the IETF website, where it can be updated one piece at a time.

subtitle: Why the IETF's guide for newcomers was retired, and what replaces it.

tldr.problem: The Tao of the IETF was the guide that explained how the IETF works to people arriving for the first time. Over thirty years it kept falling behind the community it described, and the effort of keeping it current became larger than the value it delivered.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out three reasons, updates too far apart, a single document too large to revise, and a focus on in-person meetings that no longer matched how people join.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that retires the Tao as a standalone document and obsoletes RFC 6722. The content now lives on the IETF website, and the last edition is kept in the appendix for the record.

facts.value: Never a formal IETF process document, but a community-developed and maintained informational overview

today: RFC 9592 was published in June 2024 as an Informational document. It obsoletes RFC 6722 and retires the Tao of the IETF as a single standalone document, with the last edition kept in Appendix A for archival reasons. It has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: What the Tao Was
sections.content:
Since its publication as RFC 1391 in 1993, the Tao of the IETF has described the inner workings of IETF meetings and working groups, discussed organizations related to the IETF, and introduced the working processes to new participants. The Tao was never a formal IETF process document, but rather a community-developed and maintained informational overview. After it was published as an RFC for 13 years, it was published as a webpage for over a decade, following the process described in RFC 6722.

The document did not keep up with the changes in the processes of the community and the organization, and thereby ceased to be a reliable source of information. The RFC acknowledges the individuals who contributed to the Tao over the years. It argues that the changing nature of IETF participation, a better understanding of how to most effectively convey information to new participants, and experience with publishing the Tao as a webpage all suggest a new approach to collecting, updating and communicating the information that new participants need in order to engage in the work of the IETF successfully. This document formally retires and obsoletes the Tao of the IETF as a single standalone document.
sections.plainLanguage: The Tao was never the official rulebook. It was a guide written and kept by the community to help newcomers find their way around meetings, working groups and document processes. Because it had to be updated as a whole, it was always behind.

sections.title: The Reasons for Retirement
sections.content:
The RFC gives the reasons in one line: the breadth of topics covered in the Tao, the unpredictable and different schedule for updates to the topics, and the high overhead for revising and reviewing the content did not match the needs or preferences of the intended audience of the Tao.

The three sections that follow expand on the schedule of updates, the format of the document, and the way people take part in the IETF. Taken together they describe a document that was expensive to maintain and, for that reason, was commonly out of date and did not serve its intended purpose of informing the community and newcomers.
sections.plainLanguage: One document covering everything meant everything had to be rewritten each time anything changed. The result was a guide that was right when written and stale soon after, and a heavy burden on the people who maintained it.

sections.title: Updates Too Rare to Keep Up
sections.content:
The Tao was originally published as RFC 1391 in January 1993. In the following 17 years, four additional versions were published as RFCs: RFC 1539 in October 1993, RFC 1718 in November 1994, RFC 3160 in August 2001 and RFC 4677 in September 2006.

In August 2012, RFC 6722 was published to document the process for publishing the Tao as a webpage, so that it could be updated more easily. In the subsequent 11 years, only four additional versions were published. The length of the Tao meant that review and approval of the entire document took considerable effort and time, leading to very infrequent updates.

The format was part of the problem. The large, consolidated document format made for a heavy investment by readers, in addition to the difficulty editors faced keeping pace with the changes required to keep it current. For example, the emergence of the popularity of IETF Hackathons with new participants prompted an update, but that content was effectively buried in an already long document.
sections.plainLanguage: In its first seventeen years the Tao was revised four times. When it moved to a web page in 2012, so that it could be updated more easily, it still took another eleven years to get four more versions out. A piece of news about Hackathons, for instance, arrived but sat buried inside a long page instead of being visible to the people it concerned.

sections.title: How People Join the IETF Now
sections.content:
The original Tao aimed to welcome new participants to IETF meetings, as attendance grew rapidly along with the growth of the Internet in the 1990s. As other avenues for initial participation in the IETF emerged over the ensuing decades, the main focus of the Tao remained on in-person meeting participation. Remote participation in IETF meetings has become a much more significant aspect in the past few years.

The point the RFC makes is one about the subject matter rather than the mechanics. A guide written for people arriving in a meeting room needed a lot of pages to describe the rooms, the badges and the corridors, and those pages had little to say to someone taking part from home.
sections.plainLanguage: The Tao was written for people turning up at a meeting for the first time. As other ways of joining grew, and as remote participation became normal, a guide built around the physical meeting no longer described the experience of most newcomers.

sections.title: Going Forward
sections.content:
The content of the Tao has already been integrated into the website of the IETF, which is the main channel of communication for IETF newcomers and a general audience. The content is continuously kept up to date with a variety of media to serve different audiences, and the IETF seeks to ensure that the website continues to address the needs of the ever-evolving community and potential newcomers.

The RFC then lists examples of the kinds of communication it wants to develop. These include more focused guides, for instance on Hackathon participation or on starting new work; alternative formats, such as multiple shorter documents, on-demand video and podcasts; and new channels for communication, such as blog posts, an improved Datatracker and Slack.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing was thrown away. The material now lives on the IETF website, where each piece can be changed on its own. The RFC also points at the kinds of thing that work better than one long guide: a short guide on one subject, a video you can watch when you have five minutes, and the tools the community already uses day to day.

sections.title: Conclusion and Status
sections.content:
The conclusion is that the coverage of a wide range of topics, the unpredictable and different schedule for updates, and the high overhead for revising and reviewing the content mean that the Tao required a lot of effort to maintain, was commonly out of date, and thus did not serve its intended purpose of informing the community and newcomers. The document states plainly that this is the end of the road for the Tao of the IETF and that the document is now retired. For archival reasons, the last version of the Tao can be found in the appendix of the RFC.

The Security Considerations section says the document has no security considerations, and the IANA Considerations section says the document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is retired, and the RFC keeps the final version in its appendix so that the text is not lost. There is nothing in it that changes how the network works or what any registry holds.

items.title: Infrequent updates
items.text: After 13 years as an RFC and over a decade as a web page, the Tao fell behind the processes it described.

items.title: Unwieldy format
items.text: One large consolidated document demanded a heavy investment from readers and was hard for editors to keep current.

items.title: Changing participation modes
items.text: It kept its focus on in-person meetings as other ways of joining the IETF grew, including remote participation.

items.title: Focused guides
items.text: Short guides on one subject, such as Hackathon participation or starting new work.

items.title: Alternative formats
items.text: Multiple shorter documents, on-demand video and podcasts.

items.title: New channels
items.text: Blog posts, an improved Datatracker and Slack.
